title: Amoxicillin
content: Broad-spectrum penicillin antibiotic. Indications: respiratory tract infections, otitis media, sinusitis, urinary tract infections, dental infections, H. pylori eradication. Adult dose: 500mg PO TID or 875mg BID for 7-10 days. Pediatric: 25-50 mg/kg/day divided TID. Contraindications: penicillin allergy. Monitor for rash, diarrhea, anaphylaxis.

title: Azithromycin
content: Macrolide antibiotic. Indications: community-acquired pneumonia, atypical pneumonia, pertussis, chlamydia, alternative for penicillin-allergic patients. Adult dose: 500mg PO day 1, then 250mg daily x 4 days. Pediatric: 10mg/kg day 1 then 5mg/kg daily. Contraindications: macrolide allergy, QT prolongation. Monitor for GI upset, hepatotoxicity.

title: Ciprofloxacin
content: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Indications: complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, gram-negative infections, anthrax. Adult dose: 500mg PO BID for 7-14 days. Avoid in children, pregnant women, elderly. Black box warning: tendinopathy, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects. Contraindications: tendon disorders, myasthenia gravis. Caution: QT prolongation.

title: Nitrofurantoin
content: Urinary antiseptic. Indications: uncomplicated lower UTI in women. Adult dose: 100mg PO BID for 5-7 days. Avoid: pyelonephritis, men, CrCl <30, third trimester pregnancy. Contraindications: G6PD deficiency, severe renal impairment. Monitor for pulmonary fibrosis with long-term use.

title: Ceftriaxone
content: Third-generation cephalosporin. Indications: meningitis, sepsis, severe pneumonia, gonorrhea, complicated UTI, surgical prophylaxis. Adult dose: 1-2g IV/IM daily. Pediatric: 50-100 mg/kg/day. Contraindications: cephalosporin allergy, neonates with hyperbilirubinemia. Caution: cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy in <2% of patients.

title: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)
content: Non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic. Indications: mild-moderate pain, fever. Adult dose: 500-1000mg PO every 4-6 hours, max 4g/day (3g/day if liver disease or chronic alcohol use). Pediatric: 10-15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours. Contraindications: severe hepatic impairment. Monitor: hepatotoxicity in overdose. First-line for pain in pregnancy.

title: Ibuprofen
content: NSAID. Indications: mild-moderate pain, inflammation, fever, dysmenorrhea. Adult dose: 400-600mg PO every 6-8 hours, max 2400mg/day. Contraindications: active GI bleed, severe heart failure, third trimester pregnancy, severe renal impairment, NSAID allergy. Caution: HTN, CVD, peptic ulcer history. Monitor: BP, renal function, GI bleeding.

title: Morphine
content: Strong opioid analgesic. Indications: severe acute pain, cancer pain, palliative care, MI pain. Adult dose: 5-10mg IV/IM every 4 hours; oral 10-30mg every 4 hours. Contraindications: respiratory depression, paralytic ileus, head injury without monitoring. Monitor: respiratory rate, sedation, BP. Risk: addiction, dependence, tolerance, constipation.

title: Aspirin (low-dose)
content: Antiplatelet. Indications: secondary prevention of MI/stroke, suspected ACS (load 162-325mg, then 75-100mg daily), primary prevention in selected high-risk patients. Adult dose: 75-100mg PO daily. Contraindications: active bleeding, severe asthma, children with viral illness (Reye syndrome). Monitor: bleeding signs.

title: Atorvastatin
content: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin). Indications: hyperlipidemia, primary and secondary CV prevention, post-ACS. Adult dose: 10-80mg PO daily, typically 40-80mg post-MI. Contraindications: active liver disease, pregnancy. Monitor: LFTs, CK if myalgia, lipid panel. Side effects: myalgia, rare rhabdomyolysis.

title: Lisinopril
content: ACE inhibitor. Indications: hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy. Adult dose: 10-40mg PO daily, start 5-10mg. Contraindications: pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, hyperkalemia, history of angioedema. Monitor: BP, K, creatinine 1-2 weeks after initiation. Side effects: dry cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema.

title: Metoprolol
content: Beta-1 selective blocker. Indications: HTN, angina, post-MI, heart failure (succinate), AF rate control. Adult dose: tartrate 25-100mg BID; succinate 25-200mg daily. Contraindications: severe bradycardia, decompensated heart failure, second/third-degree AV block, severe asthma. Monitor: HR, BP. Avoid abrupt discontinuation.

title: Furosemide
content: Loop diuretic. Indications: heart failure, pulmonary edema, ascites, hypertension with volume overload. Adult dose: 20-80mg PO/IV, titrate to response. Contraindications: anuria, severe hypokalemia, hypovolemia. Monitor: electrolytes (K, Na, Mg), BUN, creatinine, BP. Side effects: hypokalemia, ototoxicity (rapid IV), hypotension.

title: Warfarin
content: Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant. Indications: AF stroke prevention, VTE treatment/prevention, mechanical heart valves. Adult dose: individualized, start 5mg daily, target INR 2-3 (2.5-3.5 for mechanical mitral valve). Contraindications: pregnancy, active bleeding, recent surgery. Monitor: INR weekly until stable, then monthly. Many drug and food interactions.

title: Metformin
content: First-line oral agent for type 2 diabetes. Indications: T2DM, prediabetes, PCOS. Adult dose: start 500mg BID with meals, titrate to 1000mg BID, max 2550mg/day. Contraindications: eGFR <30, acute heart failure, severe hepatic impairment, contrast IV (hold). Monitor: B12 annually, renal function. Side effects: GI upset, rare lactic acidosis.

title: Insulin (regular and NPH)
content: Indications: T1DM (mandatory), T2DM uncontrolled on orals, DKA, HHS, gestational diabetes. Regular: rapid onset 30 min, peak 2-3 hr, duration 6-8 hr. NPH: onset 1-2 hr, peak 4-12 hr, duration 18-24 hr. Adult dose: individualized; typical T2DM start 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day basal. Monitor: glucose, HbA1c, hypoglycemia signs. Risk: hypoglycemia, weight gain.

title: Levothyroxine
content: Synthetic T4 thyroid hormone. Indications: primary and secondary hypothyroidism, myxedema coma. Adult dose: 1.6 mcg/kg/day; start lower in elderly or CVD (25-50 mcg). Take on empty stomach 30-60 min before food. Monitor: TSH 6-8 weeks after dose change, then annually. Contraindications: thyrotoxicosis. Caution: arrhythmias, osteoporosis with overtreatment.

title: Salbutamol (Albuterol)
content: Short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA). Indications: acute asthma, COPD exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchospasm. Adult dose: 100-200 mcg (1-2 puffs) MDI every 4-6 hours PRN; nebulizer 2.5-5mg every 20 min in acute exacerbation. Contraindications: hypersensitivity. Monitor: HR, K, tremor. Overuse signals poor asthma control.

title: Beclomethasone (inhaled)
content: Inhaled corticosteroid. Indications: persistent asthma, COPD with frequent exacerbations. Adult dose: 200-800 mcg/day in 2 divided doses. Onset: gradual, max benefit 4-6 weeks. Contraindications: acute bronchospasm. Side effects: oral candidiasis (rinse mouth after use), hoarseness. Long-term: rare adrenal suppression, growth velocity reduction in children.

title: Omeprazole
content: Proton pump inhibitor (PPI). Indications: GERD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori eradication, NSAID gastropathy prophylaxis, Zollinger-Ellison. Adult dose: 20-40mg PO daily, typically 30-60 min before breakfast. Long-term risks: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, increased fracture risk, C. diff infection. Avoid prolonged use without indication.

title: Ondansetron
content: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic. Indications: chemotherapy-induced nausea, postoperative nausea, hyperemesis gravidarum. Adult dose: 4-8mg PO/IV every 8 hours. Contraindications: long QT syndrome, concurrent apomorphine. Caution: QT prolongation, especially with electrolyte abnormalities. Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg.

title: Phenytoin
content: Antiepileptic. Indications: focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, status epilepticus. Adult dose: 3-5 mg/kg/day; loading 15-20 mg/kg IV. Narrow therapeutic window: 10-20 mcg/mL. Contraindications: heart block, sinus bradycardia. Monitor: levels, LFTs, CBC. Side effects: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, drug interactions (CYP inducer).

title: Diazepam
content: Benzodiazepine. Indications: status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, severe anxiety, muscle spasm, sedation. Adult dose: 2-10mg PO; status 5-10mg IV every 10-15 min, max 30mg. Contraindications: severe respiratory insufficiency, sleep apnea, myasthenia gravis. Risk: respiratory depression, dependence, paradoxical agitation in elderly.

title: Sertraline
content: SSRI antidepressant. Indications: major depression, generalized anxiety, panic, OCD, PTSD. Adult dose: 50mg daily, titrate to 50-200mg. Onset: 2-4 weeks for full effect. Contraindications: MAOI within 14 days, concurrent pimozide. Black box: increased suicidality in young adults. Monitor: mood, suicidality. Side effects: GI, sexual dysfunction, hyponatremia.

title: Haloperidol
content: First-generation antipsychotic. Indications: psychosis, acute agitation, delirium, Tourette syndrome. Adult dose: 0.5-5mg PO 2-3 times daily; acute agitation 2-10mg IM/IV. Contraindications: Parkinson disease, severe CNS depression. Black box: increased mortality in elderly with dementia. Monitor: extrapyramidal symptoms, QT, NMS.

title: Acyclovir
content: Antiviral against herpes simplex and varicella-zoster. Indications: HSV genital, oral, encephalitis; varicella; herpes zoster. Adult dose: HSV 400mg PO TID for 7-10 days; HSV encephalitis 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours; zoster 800mg PO 5x/day for 7 days. Monitor: renal function (dose adjust). Side effects: nephrotoxicity (ensure hydration), neurotoxicity in elderly.

title: Heparin (unfractionated)
content: Anticoagulant. Indications: VTE treatment, ACS, peri-procedural bridging. Adult dose: weight-based 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/hr infusion, titrated by aPTT. Contraindications: active bleeding, HIT history, severe thrombocytopenia. Monitor: aPTT every 6 hours initially, platelets (HIT). Antidote: protamine sulfate.

title: Enoxaparin
content: Low-molecular-weight heparin. Indications: VTE prophylaxis and treatment, ACS. Adult dose: prophylaxis 40mg SC daily; treatment 1 mg/kg SC BID or 1.5 mg/kg daily. Contraindications: active bleeding, severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 — use UFH instead), HIT. Monitor: anti-Xa in obese, renal impairment, pregnancy. Lower HIT risk than UFH.

title: Prednisolone
content: Systemic glucocorticoid. Indications: severe asthma exacerbation, COPD exacerbation, inflammatory/autoimmune diseases, allergic reactions. Adult dose: 30-60mg PO daily; taper if >2 weeks. Side effects: hyperglycemia, HTN, osteoporosis, immunosuppression, weight gain, mood changes. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.

title: Tetanus toxoid
content: Active immunization. Indications: routine pediatric series, adult booster every 10 years, post-exposure prophylaxis after dirty wound. Adult booster: 0.5mL IM. Wound management: TIG plus tetanus toxoid for tetanus-prone wound if last booster >5 years or unclear immunization. Contraindications: severe allergic reaction to previous dose.

content: What is a stroke?A stroke happens when there is a loss of blood flow to part of the brain. Your brain cells cannot get the oxygen and nutrients they need from blood, and they start to die within a few minutes. This can cause lasting brain damage, long-term disability, or even death.If you think that you or someone else is having a stroke, call 911 right away. Immediate treatment may save someone's life and increase the chances for successful rehabilitation

content: What is rheumatoid arthritis?Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a form of arthritis that causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints. RA is an autoimmune disease. content: What is gout?Gout is a common type of inflammatory arthritis. It causes pain, swelling, and redness in one or more joints. The flares often begin in your big toe or a lower limb.What causes gout?Gout happens when too much uric acid (urate) builds up in your body over a long time. Your body breaks down most of that food into glucose and releases it into your bloodstream. When your blood glucose goes up, it signals your pancreas to release insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps the glucose get into your cells to be used for energy.For people with diabetes, your body doesn't make enough insulin, can't use it as well as it should, or both. title: Essential Hypertension
content: The current definition of hypertension (HTN) is systolic blood pressure (SBP) values of 130 mm Hg or more and/or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of more than 80 mm Hg. Hypertension ranks among the most common chronic medical condition characterized by a persistent elevation in arterial pressure. Hypertension has been among the most studied topics of the previous century and has been one of the most significant comorbidities contributing to the development of stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and renal failure. The definition and categories of hypertension have been evolving over the years, but there is a consensus that persistent BP readings of 140/90 mm Hg or more should undergo treatment with the usual therapeutic target of 130/80 mm Hg or less. This article will attempt to review the available knowledge derived from RCTs and the recent updates and guidelines on hypertension put forward by major societies, including those from the 8th report of the Joint National Committee (JNC-8), American College of Cardiology (ACC), American Society of Hypertension (ASH), European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Society of Hypertension (ESH).

title: Stable Angina
content: Stable angina, also known as typical angina or angina pectoris, is a symptom of myocardial ischemia. Stable angina is characterized by chest discomfort or anginal equivalent that is provoked with exertion and alleviated at rest or with nitroglycerin. This is often 1 of the first manifestations or warning signs of underlying coronary disease. Angina affects 10 million people in the United States (US); given this, it is important to recognize the signs and symptoms and appropriately risk stratify and manage these individuals.

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome
content: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is among the most common diseases clinicians encounter in the inpatient setting. This syndrome comprises a spectrum of obstructive coronary artery disease that most commonly results from plaque rupture or erosion, exposing the lipid-rich core to the circulation and triggering platelet activation and the coagulation cascade, which leads to acute thrombotic occlusion. Each stage of this syndrome can be treated differently based on clinical presentation, but a catheter-based interventional approach is often preferred. For years, the primary treatment of ACS revolved around maximizing medical therapy with the use of antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy, antianginal medications, and aggressive lipid-lowering and risk factor modification. In 1958, the advent of thrombolytics shifted the paradigm in the approach and treatment of ACS. First used by Fletcher and colleagues and later validated by trials such as ISIS, GUSTO, and GISSI, intravenous thrombolytic therapy has been shown to successfully treat acute thrombotic occlusions, particularly in ST-elevated myocardial infarctions. However, even with the improvement in survival, size of the infarct, and overall morbidity, thrombolytic therapy continued to demonstrate major bleeding issues, including intracranial hemorrhage, as well as issues with reinfarction. The most effective thrombolytic regimens achieve angiographic infarct-artery patency in only 50% of patients with

title: Ischemic Stroke
content: Acute stroke is characterized by the sudden onset of focal neurological deficits within a vascular territory affecting the brain, retina, or spinal cord, caused by underlying cerebrovascular diseases. Stroke is prevalent across patient populations and is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Strokes are classified as ischemic or hemorrhagic, with hemorrhagic strokes further divided into intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages. Among ischemic strokes, the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification system is commonly used to categorize subtypes, which include: Cardioembolism. Small vessel occlusion. Large artery atherosclerosis. Stroke of undetermined etiology. Stroke of other determined etiology (possible or probable, depending on the results of ancillary studies) . A diagnosis is considered "probable" when clinical findings, neuroimaging data, and diagnostic study results consistently support a specific subtype, and other potential causes have been ruled out. On the other hand, a diagnosis is labeled "possible" when clinical findings and neuroimaging data suggest a specific subtype, but further studies have not been conducted to confirm it. As many patients undergo limited testing, these categories enable physicians to assign the most accurate subtype diagnosis possible.

title: Migraine Headache
content: Migraine is a genetically influenced complex neurological disorder characterized by episodes of moderate-to-severe headaches, typically unilateral and frequently accompanied by nausea and heightened sensitivity to light and sound. The word "migraine" is derived from the Greek word hemikrania, which was later converted into Latin as hemigranea. The French translation of the term is migraine.  Migraine is a common cause of disability and loss of work. Migraine attacks are complex and recurrent neurological events that can unfold for hours to days and significantly impact daily activities and the quality of life of individuals. The most prevalent type of migraine, accounting for 75% of cases, is migraine without aura. Subtypes of Migraine Migraines can be classified into the following subtypes according to the Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. : A migraine without aura: This subtype involves recurrent headache attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours. The pain is typically unilateral, pulsating in quality, moderate-to-severe in intensity, aggravated by physical activity, and associated with nausea, light (photophobia), and sound sensitivity (phonophobia). Migraine with aura: This subtype features recurrent, fully reversible attacks lasting minutes, typically presenting with 1 or more unilateral symptoms such as visual, sensory, speech and language, motor, brainstem, or retinal disturbances, usuall

title: Acute Kidney Injury
content: Acute kidney injury (AKI), previously called acute renal failure (ARF), denotes a sudden and often reversible reduction in kidney function, as measured by glomerular filtration rate (GFR). However, immediately after a renal insult, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or creatinine (Cr) levels may be within the normal range, and the only sign of AKI may be a decline in urine output. AKI can lead to the accumulation of water, sodium, and other metabolic products. AKI can also result in other electrolyte disturbances. AKI is a prevalent condition, especially among hospitalized patients, and can be seen in up to 7% of hospital admissions and 30% of ICU admissions. Several criteria have been used to identify AKI, such as RIFLE, AKIN (Acute Kidney Injury Network), and KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) criteria. Among these, KDIGO is the most recent and most commonly used tool. According to KDIGO, AKI is the presence of any of the following: 1. Increase in serum creatinine by 0.3 mg/dL or more (26.5 μmol/L or more) within 48 hours. 2. Increase in serum creatinine to 1.5 times or more than the baseline of the prior 7 days. 3. Urine volume less than 0.5 mL/kg/h for at least 6 hours. The RIFLE criteria define 3 categories of impairment—risk, injury, and failure—and 2 categories of long-term renal outcomes—loss and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Whichever criterion shows the most impairment is used for classificat

title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
content: Community-acquired pneumonia is a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality and incurs significant healthcare costs. As disease presentation varies from a mild illness that can be managed as an outpatient to a severe illness requiring treatment in the intensive care unit, diagnosing early and determining the appropriate level of care is important for improving outcomes.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) represents a critical metabolic emergency marked by hyperglycemia, acidosis, and ketonemia. Although most frequently associated with type 1 diabetes, the condition can also affect individuals with type 2 diabetes under certain circumstances. The severity of DKA stems from its rapid onset and potential to cause significant morbidity and mortality if unrecognized or untreated. The development of DKA commonly results from new-onset diabetes, underlying infections, or poor adherence to therapy. Additional stressors such as acute illness, trauma, or medication effects may also precipitate the condition. Early identification and prompt management remain essential, as timely intervention greatly improves patient outcomes.

title: Urinary Tract Infection
content: The anatomy of the urinary tract undergoes significant changes during pregnancy, with hormonal and mechanical factors contributing to ureteral dilation, dilation of the renal calyces, and urinary stasis, all of which predispose pregnant patients to urinary tract infections (UTIs). Progesterone relaxes smooth muscles, and the gravid uterus compresses the bladder, decreasing bladder capacity. Vesicoureteral reflux, increased residual urine in the bladder, and urinary stasis may be seen. Any of these changes lead to an increased risk of UTI in pregnancy. Typically, UTIs in pregnancy follow a predictable natural history, starting with asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), which, if left untreated, may progress to symptomatic infection, such as cystitis or pyelonephritis. The patterns of spread of UTIs in pregnancy often involve ascending infection from the lower urinary tract, facilitated by reduced urethral tone and altered bladder dynamics from pregnancy changes. Understanding these aspects is crucial for healthcare professionals to effectively recognize, diagnose, and manage UTIs in pregnancy, thereby preventing complications and ensuring optimal maternal and fetal outcomes.

title: Major Depressive Disorder
content: Major depressive disorder (MDD) has been ranked as the third cause of the burden of disease worldwide in 2008 by WHO, which has projected that this disease will rank first by 2030. It is diagnosed when an individual has a persistently low or depressed mood, anhedonia or decreased interest in pleasurable activities, feelings of guilt or worthlessness, lack of energy, poor concentration, appetite changes, psychomotor retardation or agitation, sleep disturbances, or suicidal thoughts. Per the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5), an individual must have five of the above-mentioned symptoms, of which one must be a depressed mood or anhedonia causing social or occupational impairment, to be diagnosed with MDD. History of a manic or hypomanic episode must be ruled out to make a diagnosis of MDD. Children and adolescents with MDD may present with irritable mood. Per DSM-5, other types of depression falling under the category of depressive disorders are: Persistent depressive disorder, formerly known as dysthymia. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder . Premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Substance/medication-induced depressive disorder. Depressive disorder due to another medical condition. Unspecified depressive disorder.

title: Acute Appendicitis
content: Appendicitis is characterized by inflammation of the vermiform appendix and typically presents acutely within 24 hours. However, the presenting symptoms may be more indolent and less severe in cases with perforation with a contained abscess. Notably, acute appendicitis is the leading cause of abdominal surgery in children and the most prevalent abdominal surgical emergency worldwide. The significance of this condition in terms of both pediatric and general surgery underscores the need for accurate diagnosis, prompt intervention, and appropriate management. Understanding the clinical features and distinctive nature of appendicitis is vital in providing timely care and preventing complications associated with this common condition.
